dimensions.title: Agent instructions
dimensions.question: When an agent opens this repo, does anything tell it how to use the system?
dimensions.why: An agent with no instructions falls back on habits from other libraries: shadcn imports, raw Tailwind palette classes, a local components/ui folder.

levels.1: No AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, or one that never mentions the design system.
levels.3: A file exists and names the package, but reads like a README: prose, no rules an agent can follow.
levels.5: Short and imperative: how to look a component up, how to import, which token classes are required, what is forbidden, what to run before finishing.

dimensions.title: Machine surface
dimensions.question: Can an agent query the system, or must it read files and guess?
dimensions.why: Reading .d.ts files burns context and teaches the agent the type, not the rule. A queryable surface answers the question the agent actually has.

levels.1: Nothing. Docs are a website or markdown a human reads.
levels.3: One machine-readable entry point: llms.txt, a docs CLI, or published skills.
levels.5: An MCP server or CLI that ships inside the package and answers from the installed version, so answers match the version the project has.

dimensions.title: Docs coverage
dimensions.question: Does every component a consumer can import have a guide?
dimensions.why: A component with no guide is a component the agent will either skip or reinvent, and undocumented exports are where invented APIs come from.

levels.1: Under half of the exported components have a guide.
levels.3: Most have one, and nothing stops a new component from shipping without one.
levels.5: Effectively all of them, and CI fails when a new export arrives without a guide.

dimensions.title: Docs freshness
dimensions.question: If a guide drifts from the code, does anything notice?
dimensions.why: Docs written next to the code look fine until something checks them. Guides that can only fail silently always drift.

levels.1: Guides are hand-written prose; nothing compares them to the code.
levels.3: Prop tables or examples are generated, but regenerating is a manual step somebody has to remember.
levels.5: CI regenerates the generated parts and compiles every code block in the guides against the built package. A guide that lies turns the build red.

dimensions.title: Tokens
dimensions.question: Are colour, spacing, radius and motion documented as named decisions?
dimensions.why: Without a token table the agent hardcodes hex values and raw palette classes, and every screen drifts a little further from the system.

levels.1: No token documentation; guides show raw hex or raw palette classes.
levels.3: Tokens exist and are documented, but examples still mix in raw values.
levels.5: Semantic tokens documented as tables, raw palette usage forbidden by lint, and motion and spacing covered as well as colour.

dimensions.title: Patterns
dimensions.question: Is there anything above component level — how a real page is assembled?
dimensions.why: Components tell an agent what exists. Patterns tell it what to build. Without them each agent re-invents page structure from scratch.

levels.1: Components only. Nothing describes a page.
levels.3: A pattern-to-component map: for this task, reach for these parts.
levels.5: Page-level patterns with skeleton, states and traps, loaded on demand rather than always in context.

dimensions.title: Accessibility documentation
dimensions.question: Do the guides say how a component behaves for assistive technology — keys or gestures, focus, role and name?
dimensions.why: An agent cannot infer that behaviour from a prop table alone. On the web it ships a div that looks like a menu and answers to nothing; on mobile it ships a touchable with no accessible name and no role, silent to VoiceOver and TalkBack alike.

levels.1: Accessibility is not mentioned in the guides.
levels.3: Some guides mention it, written by hand and unevenly.
levels.5: Every guide carries the full interaction contract for its platform — keys or gestures, focus or touch-target behaviour, role and naming requirements — generated from the primitives the component is built on.

dimensions.title: Verification
dimensions.question: Can an agent check its own work before calling it done?
dimensions.why: Speed is not the problem. An agent that cannot verify produces confident output nobody can audit.

levels.1: Types only, or nothing. A human is the first check.
levels.3: Unit tests and lint, run by hand.
levels.5: Every story rendered and checked for accessibility in CI, with a baseline that can only shrink, and one documented command an agent runs before finishing.

dimensions.title: Gap handling
dimensions.question: What happens when the system genuinely does not have the thing?
dimensions.why: An agent cannot tell 'this does not exist' from 'I have not found it yet', so it invents a component and moves on. More documentation cannot fix an absence.

levels.1: Nothing. The agent fills the gap silently with the nearest thing it knows.
levels.3: A written list of known absences and what to use instead.
levels.5: The list, plus an explicit stop-and-ask rule in the agent instructions, plus a way to report a new gap that lands where the next agent reads.
